header.retourAccueil: Le Domaine des Suricates, back to home

seo.titre: Le Domaine des Suricates · Zoo and wildlife park in Chartreuse
seo.description: Zoo and wildlife park in Chartreuse, France: discover meerkats and many other species at Le Domaine des Suricates. Daily feedings free to attend, dated tickets online.

hero.titre: Le Domaine des Suricates awaits you in the heart of Chartreuse
hero.texte: Meerkats and many other species live here in enclosures designed for their well-being. A zoo and wildlife park for the whole family, with daily animations free to attend.
hero.alt: A family of meerkats on the lookout on a log

habitants.titre: Meet the meerkats and their friends
habitants.texte: Our meerkats keep watch over the park, but they're not alone! Red pandas, tigers, giraffes… each species lives in an enclosure that recreates its natural habitat, in the heart of Chartreuse.

points.milieux: Enclosures inspired by the Kalahari, the savanna or the forests of Asia
points.regions: A trail organised by major regions of the world
points.famille: A walk to enjoy at your own pace, for all ages

habitants.alt: A red panda munching bamboo, perched on a log

bienEtre.texte: Here, the animals set the pace. Every day, our keepers adapt meals, care and activities to each species, so it can keep its natural behaviour.

points.repli: Spacious enclosures, with quiet spots away from view
points.enrichissement: New games and hiding places to spark their curiosity
points.veterinaire: Regular veterinary checks, and an enclosure closes whenever its residents need calm

bienEtre.alt: Two tigers rubbing heads, lying in the grass

sensibilisation.titre: Get to know them, help protect them
sensibilisation.texte: During feedings and shows, our keepers share the life of the animals in their care and the threats they face in the wild. Free, no booking needed: just come along.

points.nourrissages: Feedings with commentary every day, at set times
points.rendezVous: Special events, like the meerkat show
points.gestes: Simple things you can do, even back home

sensibilisation.alt: A keeper reaching out to a giraffe leaning over the fence

cadre.texte: WWF protects endangered species and their habitats all over the world. Discover its work and how to support it.

faq.texte: Tickets, animal talks, picnics… Here are the answers to the questions we hear most often, so you can arrive with a light heart.
faq.alt: Three giraffes, two of them calves, in their sunny enclosure, with a zebra in the foreground

billet.question: Is my ticket valid on any day?
billet.reponse: No, your ticket is dated: it is only valid on the date chosen when booking. You can book up to 12 months in advance.

animations.question: Do I need to book the animal talks?
animations.reponse: Not at all! Feedings and shows are free and open to all. Just be there at the time shown in the programme: kids love them.

duree.question: How long should we plan for?
duree.reponse: Allow half a day to tour the park, or a full day to enjoy the feedings and animal talks. Last entry one hour before closing.

repas.question: Where can we eat during the visit?
repas.reponse: Picnic areas await you all along the trail, as well as food outlets for small appetites and anyone as hungry as a wolf.

groupes.question: Coming as a group (school, holiday club, association)?
groupes.reponse: Give us a call before your visit: we'll plan it with you and adapt our welcome to your group, with a dedicated rate.

animations.titre: Something new to see every day
animations.texte: Cheetahs at dinnertime, red pandas at snack time, birds of prey swooping over the stands… Our keepers bring you into the daily lives of the animals in their care. It's free, no booking needed: just be there at the right time.
animations.aucune: No activities in this area for now: see the full park programme below.

zones.titre: The five regions of the world to explore
zones.texte: From the Kalahari desert to the forests of Asia, a visit to the Domaine is like a little trip around the world. Find the paths and facilities before you set off.
zones.planAlt: Illustrated map of the Domaine's pedestrian area: coloured areas linked by paths, with restaurants, shops, toilets, picnic areas, the first-aid post and car parks.

restauration.texte: Five places to eat, from the ice-cream stand to the self-service.

parkings.texte: Spaces reserved for people with reduced mobility, and bike parking.

horairesTarifs.intro: Open almost all year round in Chartreuse, Le Domaine des Suricates adapts its opening hours to the seasons. Book your dated ticket online, or buy it on site on the day.
horairesTarifs.alt: A meerkat standing on its hind legs keeps watch on a tree stump

reduit.condition: Ages 3 to 12 and people with disabilities

seo.titre: The park · Le Domaine des Suricates
seo.description: Five regions of the world to explore at the Domaine des Suricates: African savannahs, Asian forests, the Andes and ocean shores. Discover the park's areas and their residents.

hero.texte: At the Domaine, our keepers work right alongside the animals. Follow the paths at your own pace, from one region of the world to the next, and find out who lives in each enclosure.
hero.alt: A keeper strokes the muzzle of a rhino chewing leaves over the wooden fence

zones.titre: A little trip around the world in five regions
zones.texte: From the savannahs of Africa to the forests of Asia, each area recreates its residents' habitat. Pick your next stop and start exploring!

chemin-de-brousse.accroche: Elephants, giraffes and zebras share the shade of the acacias, while rhinos roll in the mud and meerkats keep watch. Welcome to the savannah!
chemin-de-brousse.milieu: Grassy plains, termite mounds and umbrella acacias: the savannah stretches out to the watering holes where everyone comes to cool off.
chemin-de-brousse.habitants: Elephants, rhinos and giraffes live alongside ostriches, meerkats and a lively troop of lemurs.
chemin-de-brousse.alt: Two giraffes and a zebra with its foal in the shade of a large tree on the savannah
chemin-de-brousse.altHero: An elephant calf wraps its trunk around an adult elephant's trunk on muddy ground

milieuNaturel.titre: To the rhythm of the African savannah
milieuNaturel.texte: On the great plains of eastern and southern Africa, all life revolves around the watering holes. Elephants dig into the ground to drink, giraffes pick the highest acacia leaves and ostriches race along at nearly 70 km/h.
milieuNaturel.region: Eastern and southern Africa, all the way to the island of Madagascar.
milieuNaturel.climat: Hot and dry, with short rainy seasons that turn the plains green again.
milieuNaturel.paysage: Grassy plains, umbrella acacias, termite mounds and watering holes.

habitantsSection.titre: The animals of the Bush Trail
habitantsSection.texte: Under the acacias of the Bush Trail, every species has its own character, habits and favourite spot. Meerkats on guard, elephants as a family, giraffes on the lookout: meet the animals that bring the savannah to life at Le Domaine des Suricates, in the Chartreuse mountains.

conservation.texte: At Le Domaine des Suricates, discovering the animals of the Bush Trail also means supporting their conservation. Here is how our wildlife park takes action for giraffes, rhinos and their neighbours.

territoire-des-fauves.accroche: Here, the predators rule. From the lookout towers, spot the tiger patrolling the tall grass, the cheetah ready to pounce or the pack of African wild dogs taking a nap.
territoire-des-fauves.milieu: Tall grass, sun-warmed rocks and wooden lookout towers: watch the big cats without them noticing you.
territoire-des-fauves.habitants: Lions, tigers and cheetahs share the territory with hyenas, African wild dogs and a family of gorillas.
territoire-des-fauves.alt: A lion with a golden mane lying on a rock in the sun
territoire-des-fauves.altHero: A tiger sitting in the sun in front of a stone wall, gazing into the distance

milieuNaturel.titre: On the trail of the great predators
milieuNaturel.texte: From the savannahs of Africa to the forests of Asia, every predator has its own technique: the cheetah sprints, the tiger happily swims and African wild dogs hunt in packs. In the shade, the gorillas spend their days nibbling leaves and fruit.
milieuNaturel.region: African savannahs, Central African forests and the jungles of South Asia.
milieuNaturel.climat: Tropical, with a distinct dry season and rainy season.
milieuNaturel.paysage: Tall grass, rocky outcrops and the edge of dense forest.

habitantsSection.titre: The animals of Big Cat Territory
habitantsSection.texte: In Big Cat Territory, the great predators of Africa and Asia live in large enclosures designed for their well-being. Lazy lions, swimming tigers, well-organised hyenas: each has its own way of owning the territory.

conservation.texte: Lions, tigers, cheetahs and wild dogs are threatened in the wild. In the Big Cat Territory, Le Domaine des Suricates acts for their future, at the park and in the field.

temple-de-la-jungle.accroche: Step into a bamboo forest where time slows down. The giant panda munches away, gibbons sing in the trees and otters play in the streams.
temple-de-la-jungle.milieu: Bamboo, streams and red gateways: a cool, quiet Asian forest, perfect on hot days.
temple-de-la-jungle.habitants: Giant and red pandas, singing gibbons, binturongs, otters and muntjacs share the forest.
temple-de-la-jungle.alt: A giant panda munching a bamboo stalk among the greenery
temple-de-la-jungle.altHero: A giant panda sitting on a fallen log, surrounded by leaves

milieuNaturel.titre: In the misty forests of Asia
milieuNaturel.texte: In the misty mountains of China, the giant panda spends up to 12 hours a day eating bamboo. Further south, the jungle belongs to the climbers: gibbons, red pandas and binturongs spend almost their whole lives in the trees.
milieuNaturel.region: The mountains of central China, the Himalayas and Southeast Asia.
milieuNaturel.climat: Cool and damp in the mountains, hot and rainy in the valleys.
milieuNaturel.paysage: Bamboo forests, mountain streams and a thick canopy.

habitantsSection.titre: The animals of the Jungle Temple
habitantsSection.texte: Among bamboo and overgrown ruins, the Jungle Temple is home to Asian species as discreet as they are surprising. Hungry pandas, singing gibbons, popcorn-scented binturongs: come and meet them.

conservation.titre: Protecting the animals of Asia's forests
conservation.texte: Pandas, gibbons and binturongs depend on forests that are disappearing. In the Jungle Temple, Le Domaine des Suricates is committed to their conservation.

sentier-des-incas.accroche: Walk through the great Inca gate and follow the trail to the lagoons. Capybaras, flamingos and colourful macaws await you along the water.
sentier-des-incas.milieu: Walk through the Inca gate and follow a path between lagoons and rainforest, just like in the Amazon.
sentier-des-incas.habitants: Llamas and alpacas up high, tapirs, capybaras and squirrel monkeys in the forest, flamingos on the lagoons.
sentier-des-incas.alt: A hornbill with a large yellow beak perched on a branch in front of a wooden fence
sentier-des-incas.altHero: A capybara and its young sitting side by side on the grass in the sun

milieuNaturel.titre: From the Andes to the Amazon
milieuNaturel.texte: On the high plateaus of the Andes, llamas and alpacas make do with short grass. Heading down towards the Amazon, you meet the flamingos of the lagoons, then the capybara, the world's largest rodent, which never strays far from water.
milieuNaturel.region: South America, from the Andes mountains to the Amazon basin.
milieuNaturel.climat: Cold and dry at altitude, hot and very humid in the Amazon.
milieuNaturel.paysage: High plateaus, shallow lagoons and tropical forest.

habitantsSection.titre: The animals of the Inca Trail
habitantsSection.texte: From the peaks of the Andes to the lagoons of the Amazon, the Inca Trail brings together the animals of South America. Chatty llamas, unflappable capybaras, dazzling macaws: each adds its own touch to the journey.

conservation.texte: Tapirs, macaws and monkeys live in forests that shrink every year. Along the Inca Trail, Le Domaine des Suricates is committed to their protection.

cite-marine.accroche: Splashes guaranteed! Around the big pools, sea lions dive again and again, pelicans keep an eye out for fish and penguins waddle along their pebble beach.
cite-marine.milieu: Large clear-water pools and pebble beaches, with windows to watch them underwater.
cite-marine.habitants: Chatty sea lions, seals, playful dolphins, pelicans and penguins, true masters of the glide.
cite-marine.alt: Three sea lions leap out of the water in front of stands full of spectators
cite-marine.altHero: A group of Humboldt penguins on a pebble beach by the water

milieuNaturel.texte: Where cold currents make the ocean rich in fish, sea lions and penguins split their lives between fishing at sea and resting on the pebbles. Out at sea, dolphins follow the shoals of fish, talking to each other with whistles.
milieuNaturel.region: Pacific and Atlantic coasts, from temperate waters to cold seas.
milieuNaturel.climat: Cool and oceanic, with cold water all year round.
milieuNaturel.paysage: Rocky coasts, pebble beaches and open sea.

habitantsSection.titre: The animals of the Marine City
habitantsSection.texte: Pools, pebble beaches and rocks: the Marine City welcomes animals from the coasts and oceans. Chatty sea lions, torpedo penguins, fishing pelicans: discover what makes each of them unique.

conservation.texte: Dolphins, seals and penguins depend on healthy oceans. In the Marine City, Le Domaine des Suricates is committed to their protection.

enclos.heroTexte: Watch them up close along your walk: discover their daily life at the Domaine, their natural habitat and everything that makes them who they are. Our keepers look after their well-being every day, in enclosures designed for them. An encounter to enjoy as a family, at your own pace.

seo.titre: {nom} at Le Domaine des Suricates, wildlife park in Chartreuse
seo.description: Come and see our {effectif} {nom} in {zone}, at the heart of our wildlife park in Chartreuse. Origin, diet, feeding times: everything to know before your visit.

rendezVous.sans: No show for now: watch them quietly, at any time of day.

voisins.texte: Keep exploring: these species live just next door.

identite.texte: Where do they come from, what do they eat, how many live at the Domaine? Their ID card gathers everything worth knowing before your visit. And to shine on your walk, a surprising fun fact awaits right next to it: enough to amaze young and old alike in front of the enclosure.

suricates.texte: While the colony digs its burrows, one of them always stands on its hind legs to watch the sky. Our mascots have a different call for every danger.
suricates.anecdote: Meerkats are immune to some scorpion venoms, and adults teach the young to remove the sting before eating.
suricates.vedette: At the park, the colony has a large heated sand burrow to dig in as much as they like. Come in the morning, when the whole gang comes out to sunbathe, tummies turned towards the rays.

elephants.texte: Led by the matriarch, the family moves as one and greets each other trunk to trunk. Their daily dust bath is quite a show.
elephants.anecdote: An elephant can eat up to 150 kg of plants a day and drink almost 200 litres of water.
elephants.vedette: Their enclosure stretches around a large pool where they splash and bathe as soon as the sun comes out. In late morning, keepers scatter fresh branches: the perfect time to watch them at work.

girafes.texte: Standing 5 metres tall, they spot anything that moves on the savannah. Their 45 cm blue tongue grabs the highest acacia leaves.
girafes.origine: Savannahs of eastern and southern Africa
girafes.anecdote: A giraffe sleeps only 30 minutes to 2 hours a day, often in short naps standing up.
girafes.vedette: At the park, their feeders are set up high to match the way they naturally eat. From the walkway, you'll see them almost eye to eye.

zebres.texte: No two zebras share the same stripes: it's their fingerprint. Foals recognise their mother by her pattern.
zebres.origine: Plains of eastern and southern Africa
zebres.anecdote: Their stripes seem to confuse biting flies, which struggle to land on a striped coat.
zebres.vedette: They share the great plain with the giraffes, just like on the savannah. Watch the herd closely: everyone has their rank, and the foals never leave their mother's side.

rhinoceros.texte: Over two tonnes of calm who swear by their mud bath, a natural sunscreen. Their eyesight is poor, but they never forget a smell.
rhinoceros.anecdote: Their horn is made of keratin, the same material as our nails and hair.
rhinoceros.vedette: Their enclosure has several mud wallows kept up by the keepers. They love being brushed, which is also a gentle way to check on their health.

lemuriens.texte: Every morning the troop sits arms wide open facing the sun to warm up. Their long striped tail works as a rallying flag.
lemuriens.anecdote: Lemurs live in the wild only in Madagascar and nowhere else on the planet.
lemuriens.vedette: At the park, the troop lives on a wooded island surrounded by water, with no fences. Don't be surprised to see them leaping from tree to tree right above the path.

autruches.texte: The world's largest bird can't fly, but races at 70 km/h on just two toes. Its eye is bigger than its brain.
autruches.anecdote: The ostrich egg, the largest in the world, weighs as much as about twenty hen's eggs.
autruches.vedette: Their large sandy run gives them plenty of room for a sprint. Come close to the fence: they're very curious and will probably come over to look at you.

lions.texte: The pride spends up to 20 hours a day resting in the shade. The male's roar carries over 8 kilometres; you can sometimes hear it from the entrance.
lions.anecdote: Lionesses do most of the hunting, as a team and with a real encircling strategy.
lions.vedette: The pride has its favourite heated rocks, from which it watches over the whole territory. Best time to see them active? Late in the day, when the heat drops.

tigres.texte: Unlike other big cats, our tigers love water and dive in as soon as it gets warm. Their stripes go all the way down to their skin.
tigres.origine: Forests of South and Southeast Asia
tigres.anecdote: The tiger is the largest cat in the world: some males are over 3 metres long.
tigres.vedette: Their wooded enclosure has a large pool where they come to cool off. With a little patience at the viewing window, you might see them dive just a few metres away.

guepards.texte: From 0 to 100 km/h in three seconds, but only over short distances. The black tear marks under their eyes cut the glare.
guepards.origine: Savannahs of eastern and southern Africa
guepards.anecdote: Unlike other big cats, cheetahs can't roar: they meow, purr and make little chirping sounds.
guepards.vedette: At the park, they have a long grassy track to stretch their legs. Don't miss their feeding time, one of the highlights of the day.

gorilles.texte: A calm, watchful family guided by an imposing silverback. Every evening they build a brand-new nest for the night.
gorilles.anecdote: Gorillas share about 98% of their DNA with us.
gorilles.vedette: The family lives in a large planted space with ropes, hammocks and a heated shelter. Keepers hide fruit and vegetables there to keep them busy and curious.

hyenes.texte: Far more organised than their reputation: females lead the clan. Their famous laugh is mostly a way of talking.
hyenes.anecdote: The spotted hyena has one of the most powerful jaws in the animal kingdom, strong enough to crush bone.
hyenes.vedette: Their enclosure is designed for a clan, with several dens and lookout points. Listen carefully: their calls often ring out in the early evening.

lycaons.texte: Each dog has a unique spotted coat, and the pack shares absolutely everything, starting with meals. They even vote to set off by sneezing.
lycaons.origine: Savannahs of southern and East Africa
lycaons.anecdote: The African wild dog is one of Africa's most efficient hunters: nearly 8 hunts out of 10 succeed.
lycaons.vedette: The pack lives on a large hilly area where it always moves as one. It's one of Africa's most endangered species, and the park takes part in its conservation.

pandas-geants.texte: They spend almost half their day munching bamboo, sitting as if in an armchair. A false thumb helps them hold every stalk.
pandas-geants.anecdote: A giant panda eats between 12 and 38 kg of bamboo a day to meet its needs.
pandas-geants.vedette: At the park, their bamboo is delivered fresh several times a week. Each has its own space, with climbing frames, a pool and a cool corner for hot days.

pandas-roux.texte: Closer to raccoons than to giant pandas, they live their whole life in the branches. Their bushy tail doubles as a winter scarf.
pandas-roux.anecdote: The red panda was named 'panda' fifty years before the giant panda.
pandas-roux.vedette: Look up as you walk through their enclosure: they like to rest at the very top of the branches. They're most active in the morning and late afternoon.

loutres.texte: Always on the move, they juggle pebbles and hold hands to sleep in the water. A real bundle of energy.
loutres.origine: Rivers and mangroves of Southeast Asia
loutres.anecdote: An otter can have up to 100,000 hairs per square centimetre, the densest fur in the animal kingdom.
loutres.vedette: Their gently flowing river runs right through the enclosure, with a window to watch them underwater. Children love watching them slide around.

gibbons.texte: Every morning the pair sings a duet that echoes throughout the temple. They swing from branch to branch without ever touching the ground.
gibbons.anecdote: A gibbon can cover 10 metres in a single leap while swinging from branch to branch.
gibbons.vedette: They live on a tree-covered island fitted with long vines for swinging. Arrive early to hear their song, which marks the start of the day at the Temple.

binturongs.texte: Half cat, half bear, they sleep by day and hang on to branches with their tail. Their surprising scent smells like warm popcorn.
binturongs.anecdote: Binturongs help forests grow by spreading the seeds of the figs they eat.
binturongs.vedette: They spend the day dozing high up in their tropical enclosure. Come closer quietly: their popcorn scent often gives them away.

muntjacs.texte: These little deer slip through the undergrowth and bark like dogs to sound the alarm. Keep your eyes peeled to spot them.
muntjacs.origine: Forests of South and East Asia
muntjacs.anecdote: Male muntjacs have small antlers and two long canines that stick out from their lip.
muntjacs.vedette: Their dense undergrowth offers plenty of hiding places, just like their native forest. A real treasure hunt for sharp-eyed visitors!

lamas.texte: Curious and a little chatty, they talk to each other with soft humming. In the Andes, they have carried loads for centuries.
lamas.anecdote: Llamas spit to defend themselves, but mostly at each other, rarely at humans.
lamas.vedette: Their sloping enclosure recalls the Andes, with a view of the Chartreuse mountains. They're perfectly at home in our cool winters.

alpagas.texte: Their wool, among the softest in the world, keeps out the cold of the peaks. Smaller than llamas, they always live in groups.
alpagas.anecdote: Alpacas use a shared 'toilet spot', which makes the keepers' job much easier.
alpagas.vedette: They share the high ground with the llamas. Every spring, keepers shear them to keep them comfortable before the hot weather.

tapirs.texte: Their small trunk-like nose works as a snorkel when they swim. Calves are born striped and spotted, like watermelons.
tapirs.anecdote: Tapirs have been around for over 20 million years with hardly any change in appearance.
tapirs.vedette: Their pool is deep enough for proper dives. Keepers often give them floating fruit, much to their delight.

capybaras.texte: The world's largest rodents spend hours in the water, completely unbothered. Other animals happily settle down next to them.
capybaras.anecdote: Capybaras can stay underwater for up to 5 minutes to escape danger.
capybaras.vedette: They live by a large pond that they happily share with the birds. Watching them doze in the water, eyes half closed, is pure relaxation.

saimiris.texte: Lively, curious little monkeys that always move as a group, passing on the news with high-pitched calls.
saimiris.anecdote: Squirrel monkeys live in groups that can number several dozen individuals.
saimiris.vedette: Their tropical aviary is a real playground, with ropes and tangled branches. There's always something going on.

flamants.texte: Their bright pink comes from the tiny shrimp they filter from the water. They sleep standing on one leg without ever losing their balance.
flamants.anecdote: Flamingos eat upside down, filtering water through their curved beak.
flamants.vedette: The colony lives on a shallow lagoon in the heart of the Inca Trail. In spring, don't miss their courtship parades, when the whole flock marches in step.

aras.texte: Dazzling feathers, a beak that cracks the toughest nuts and a voice that carries through the forest. Pairs stay together for life.
aras.anecdote: Some macaws can live for more than 60 years.
aras.vedette: They live in a large aviary where they can fly freely. They're very chatty too, so listen out!

otaries.texte: Nimble in the water and on the rocks, they walk on their flippers and never stop talking. Their small ears set them apart from seals.
otaries.anecdote: Sea lions can turn their hind flippers under their body to walk, something seals can't do.
otaries.vedette: Their large seawater pool has rocks and a beach. Medical training sessions with the keepers are open to the public: a special moment you shouldn't miss.

phoques.texte: They bask in the sun between dives and can hold their breath for half an hour. On land, they wriggle along like caterpillars.
phoques.anecdote: A seal's whiskers are so sensitive they can detect the wake of a fish in the water.
phoques.vedette: They share the Marine City with the sea lions, but in a pool of their own. Watch them through the underwater window: that's where they're at their most graceful.

dauphins.texte: Playful and very social, they recognise each other by a unique whistle, like a name. They only ever sleep with half their brain.
dauphins.anecdote: Dolphins find their way using echolocation: they 'see' with sound.
dauphins.vedette: Their deep lagoon lets them swim, leap and play at their own pace. Keepers offer them new games every day to keep them curious.

manchots.texte: Clumsy on land, they turn into rockets underwater. Each pair finds the other in the middle of the colony by its call.
manchots.anecdote: Underwater, African penguins can swim at almost 20 km/h.
manchots.vedette: Their pebble beach overlooks a clear-water pool. At mealtime, the whole colony rushes towards the keepers: an irresistible sight.

pelicans.texte: Their big pouched bill can hold more water than their stomach. They fish as a team, herding the fish in a single move.
pelicans.origine: Lakes and coasts of Europe and Africa
pelicans.anecdote: A pelican's pouch can hold up to 11 litres of water.
pelicans.vedette: They live on a large stretch of water where they catch their fish. Watch them spread their wings, nearly 3 metres across!

hippopotames.texte: They spend the day underwater and only come out to graze at nightfall. Their spectacular yawn is mostly a way of standing their ground.
hippopotames.origine: Rivers and lakes of sub-Saharan Africa
hippopotames.anecdote: Their skin secretes a reddish fluid that works as a natural sunscreen.
hippopotames.vedette: At the park, their heated pool has a window to watch them underwater, where they walk more than they swim.

gnous.texte: Bearded and a little gangly, they live in a close-knit herd. In the wild, they travel thousands of kilometres every year.
gnous.anecdote: A wildebeest calf stands within minutes of birth and runs with the herd within the hour.
gnous.vedette: They share the great plain with the zebras, their migration companions on the savannah.

phacocheres.texte: They graze on their knees, resting on calluses that protect their front legs. When they run, their tail sticks straight up like an antenna.
phacocheres.anecdote: The 'warts' on their head are actually skin pads that protect their eyes during fights.
phacocheres.vedette: Their sandy enclosure is full of burrows, which they back into, tusks facing out.

babouins.texte: A noisy, highly organised troop where everyone knows their place. Grooming each other takes up a good part of their day.
babouins.anecdote: Baboons use more than thirty different calls to communicate.
babouins.vedette: Their rocky hill offers plenty of perches: look up, the lookout is never far away.

oryx.texte: Their long straight horns and black-and-white mask make them unforgettable. They can bear extreme heat without drinking for days.
oryx.anecdote: Oryx can let their body temperature rise to save the water they would lose by sweating.
oryx.vedette: They live in the driest part of the Bush Trail, among sand and rocks.

servals.texte: With their huge ears, they can hear a rodent moving under the grass. Their vertical leap can top 3 metres.
servals.anecdote: Servals have the longest legs of any cat relative to their size.
servals.vedette: Their tall-grass enclosure lets them practise their famous hunting pounce.

calaos.texte: The casque on top of their beak gives them a prehistoric look. They often move along the ground in little hops.
calaos.anecdote: In some hornbill species, the female seals herself into the nest and the male feeds her through a slit.
calaos.vedette: They live in an aviary near the meerkats, with whom they get along well in the wild.

marabouts.texte: These bald-headed waders are the savannah's clean-up crew. Their stern look hides very sociable birds.
marabouts.anecdote: Their wingspan can reach 3 metres, one of the largest of any bird.
marabouts.vedette: They stroll along the watering hole, often standing still like statues.

springboks.texte: These small gazelles bounce on the spot, back arched and legs stiff, as if on springs. Quite a show when the group gets excited.
springboks.anecdote: Their leaps can reach 2 metres high: it's called 'pronking'.
springboks.vedette: They share the plain with the zebras and wildebeest, and love a morning run.

tortues-sillonnees.texte: Africa's largest mainland tortoise can weigh over 80 kg. It digs deep burrows to escape the heat.
tortues-sillonnees.anecdote: A sulcata tortoise can live for more than 80 years.
tortues-sillonnees.vedette: At the park, they have a heated shelter and come out for a stroll as soon as the sun is strong.

leopards.texte: Stealthy and powerful, they haul their prey up into trees to keep it safe. Every leopard has unique rosettes.
leopards.anecdote: A leopard can carry prey heavier than itself up a tree.
leopards.vedette: Look up in their wooded enclosure: they spend a lot of time lying on the branches.

pantheres-des-neiges.texte: Ghosts of the mountains, they wrap themselves in their long thick tail to keep warm. They can't roar.
pantheres-des-neiges.anecdote: Their broad furry paws work like snowshoes.
pantheres-des-neiges.vedette: Their steep rocky enclosure recalls the peaks: Chartreuse winters suit them perfectly.

caracals.texte: Recognisable by the long black tufts on their ears, they are exceptional jumpers.
caracals.anecdote: A caracal can catch a bird in flight with a 3-metre leap.
caracals.vedette: Their dry, rocky enclosure is dotted with high lookout posts.

chimpanzes.texte: Our closest cousins use tools, make up with a hug and laugh when they play.
chimpanzes.origine: Forests of Central and West Africa
chimpanzes.anecdote: Chimpanzees use twigs to 'fish' termites out of their nest.
chimpanzes.vedette: The community lives on a large wooded island with ropes and nets. Keepers hide puzzles there to solve for treats.

mandrills.texte: The most colourful primate has a red and blue face, all the brighter when the male is dominant.
mandrills.anecdote: A male's colours fade if he loses his rank in the group.
mandrills.vedette: Their group lives in a dense forest where they forage on the ground for food.

ours-malais.texte: The smallest bear has a 25 cm tongue to reach honey and termites. It wears a golden patch on its chest.
ours-malais.anecdote: Every sun bear's chest patch is different, like a signature.
ours-malais.vedette: They happily climb the trees in their enclosure and nap in a hammock.

dholes.texte: These red-coated wild dogs of Asia communicate by whistling. The pack lets the young eat first.
dholes.origine: Forests of South and East Asia
dholes.anecdote: They're nicknamed 'whistling dogs' because of their calls.
dholes.vedette: They live as a pack on wooded, hilly ground, always on the move.

fennecs.texte: The world's smallest fox has the largest ears for its size. They help it hear and keep cool.
fennecs.anecdote: Fennec foxes can go without drinking: they get water from their food.
fennecs.vedette: Their warm sandy enclosure lets them dig burrows with several entrances.

chacals.texte: Loyal to their partner for life, they raise their pups with help from older siblings.
chacals.anecdote: Black-backed jackals are named after the dark saddle on their back.
chacals.vedette: They share the big cats' savannah, at a safe distance from the lions.

pantheres-nebuleuses.texte: They have the longest canines of any cat relative to their size. Their large spots look like clouds.
pantheres-nebuleuses.anecdote: They can climb down a tree head first thanks to very flexible ankles.
pantheres-nebuleuses.vedette: Their densely planted enclosure is mostly vertical: they live in the trees.

orangs-outans.texte: Thoughtful red giants, they build a leafy nest every evening. Youngsters stay with their mother until they're 8.
orangs-outans.anecdote: Their name comes from Malay and means 'person of the forest'.
orangs-outans.vedette: Their large covered space offers vines and high platforms, just like the canopy.

dragons-de-komodo.texte: The world's largest lizard can be over 2.5 metres long. It 'tastes' the air with its forked tongue.
dragons-de-komodo.anecdote: Females can lay viable eggs without a male.
dragons-de-komodo.vedette: Their heated enclosure recreates the warmth of their islands: they love basking under the lamps.

paons.texte: The male fans out over 150 eye-spotted feathers to win a mate. The peahens do the choosing.
paons.origine: Forests of India and Sri Lanka
paons.anecdote: Peacocks shed their long feathers every year and grow a full new set.
paons.vedette: They roam freely around the Temple, so don't be surprised to meet one on the path.

tapirs-malais.texte: Their black and white coat makes them invisible in the forest at night. They are excellent swimmers.
tapirs-malais.anecdote: Calves are born striped and spotted, then get their two-tone coat at around 6 months.
tapirs-malais.vedette: They live by a shady pool where they spend much of the day.

entelles.texte: These grey monkeys with black faces are sacred in India. They live in close-knit troops.
entelles.anecdote: Their multi-chambered stomach lets them digest leaves that would poison other animals.
entelles.vedette: Their rocky, wooded enclosure recalls the temple ruins where they're seen in India.

loris.texte: Small nocturnal primates with huge round eyes, they move with surprising slowness.
loris.anecdote: The slow loris is one of the few venomous primates: a gland on its elbow produces the venom.
loris.vedette: You'll find them in the Temple's night house, where the lighting is reversed so you can see them active.

pythons.texte: These large non-venomous snakes ambush and constrict their prey. They can go months without eating.
pythons.anecdote: Pythons sense the heat of their prey through pits along their lips.
pythons.vedette: Their tropical terrarium is kept at 30 °C, with a pool they like to slip into.

nasiques.texte: The male has an enormous nose that amplifies his calls. They're also strong swimmers with webbed feet.
nasiques.anecdote: The bigger the male's nose, the more attractive he is to females.
nasiques.vedette: Their enclosure borders a river: they don't hesitate to dive in from the branches.

gavials.texte: Their very slender snout, lined with about a hundred teeth, is built to snap up fish with a flick of the head.
gavials.anecdote: Males have a bulb on the tip of their snout called a 'ghara', after an Indian pot.
gavials.vedette: They live in the Temple's large pool and bask on the bank in late morning.

gaurs.texte: The world's largest wild cattle can weigh over a tonne. Despite its size, it's rather shy.
gaurs.origine: Forests of India and Southeast Asia
gaurs.anecdote: Their legs look as if they're wearing white socks.
gaurs.vedette: They live in a bamboo-fringed clearing at the entrance to the Temple.

jaguars.texte: The largest cat in the Americas has the most powerful bite of all. It happily swims and hunts in water.
jaguars.origine: Forests of Central and South America
jaguars.anecdote: Jaguar rosettes often have a small dot in the middle, unlike a leopard's.
jaguars.vedette: Their rainforest enclosure is crossed by a river where they come to fish and cool off.

tamanoirs.texte: This anteater has no teeth but a 60 cm tongue, which it flicks out up to 150 times a minute.
tamanoirs.origine: Grasslands and forests of South America
tamanoirs.anecdote: A giant anteater can swallow up to 35,000 ants a day.
tamanoirs.vedette: They roam their enclosure sniffing every corner: keepers hide stocked termite mounds there.

paresseux.texte: Champions of slowness, they sleep up to 15 hours a day upside down. Algae sometimes grow in their fur.
paresseux.anecdote: A sloth only comes down from its tree about once a week, to go to the toilet.
paresseux.vedette: They live in the tropical greenhouse, hanging just above visitors: look for them in the branches.

tatous.texte: Protected by a jointed shell, they're tireless diggers with a keen sense of smell.
tatous.anecdote: The three-banded armadillo can roll into a perfect ball to protect itself.
tatous.vedette: Their sandy enclosure is full of tunnels; they're most active late in the day.

toucans.texte: Their huge, colourful bill is surprisingly light. They use it to pick fruit at the tips of branches.
toucans.anecdote: Their bill helps regulate their body temperature, like a radiator.
toucans.vedette: They fly freely in the tropical greenhouse, among the macaws and squirrel monkeys.

condors.texte: With a wingspan of over 3 metres, they soar for hours above the peaks without flapping once.
condors.anecdote: Andean condors can live for more than 70 years.
condors.vedette: Their huge high aviary looks out over the Chartreuse: you'll often see them with wings spread in the sun.

vigognes.texte: The wild ancestors of alpacas have one of the finest wools in the world.
vigognes.anecdote: In Inca times, only the royal family could wear vicuña wool.
vigognes.vedette: They share the heights of the Trail with the llamas and alpacas.

nandous.texte: South American cousins of the ostrich, they can't fly but run very fast in zigzags.
nandous.anecdote: The male rhea incubates the eggs and raises the chicks on his own.
nandous.vedette: They roam the Trail's big meadow, often alongside the capybaras.

tamarins.texte: These tiny monkeys with white moustaches live in families where everyone carries the babies.
tamarins.anecdote: Tamarins very often give birth to twins.
tamarins.vedette: Their planted aviary is full of thin branches where they dart about at full speed.

loups-a-criniere.texte: Perched on very long legs, they look like foxes on stilts. They live alone.
loups-a-criniere.anecdote: More than half their diet is fruit, especially the 'wolf apple'.
loups-a-criniere.vedette: They roam their tall-grass meadow mostly at dusk.

tortues-marines.texte: They travel thousands of kilometres across the oceans and return to lay eggs on the beach where they hatched.
tortues-marines.anecdote: The temperature of the sand decides whether baby turtles are male or female.
tortues-marines.vedette: Ours were rescued after injuries; they live in the large pool and take part in care programmes.

requins.texte: Far from the clichés, they are discreet animals, essential to the health of the oceans.
requins.anecdote: A shark replaces its teeth throughout its life and can go through thousands.
requins.vedette: They glide through the big aquarium, which you cross through a glass tunnel.

raies.texte: They 'fly' underwater by rippling their large fins. Some hide under the sand with only their eyes showing.
raies.anecdote: Rays sense the electric field of prey hidden under the sand.
raies.vedette: Their shallow touch pool lets you see them up close, with a keeper.

meduses.texte: With no brain or heart, they've been around for over 500 million years. Their hypnotic dance is quite a sight.
meduses.anecdote: Some jellyfish can reverse their ageing and start their life cycle again.
meduses.vedette: They drift in softly lit round tanks in the heart of the Marine City.

poissons-clowns.texte: They live sheltered in sea anemones, whose mucus protects them from stings. Each anemone is home to a small family.
poissons-clowns.origine: Reefs of the Indian Ocean and Pacific
poissons-clowns.anecdote: All clownfish are born male; the largest of the group can become female.
poissons-clowns.vedette: Their recreated reef is bursting with colour: children always stop there.

loutres-de-mer.texte: They float on their backs, crack shellfish on their tummy with a stone and sleep holding hands.
loutres-de-mer.anecdote: Each sea otter keeps its favourite stone in a pouch of skin under its arm.
loutres-de-mer.vedette: Their cold-water pool has rocks and an underwater window.

macareux.texte: With their multicoloured bill, they're nicknamed 'sea parrots'. They fly and swim with equal ease.
macareux.anecdote: A puffin can hold more than ten fish in its bill at once.
macareux.vedette: Their recreated cliff overlooks a cold-water pool where they dive for fish.

morses.texte: They use their long tusks to haul themselves onto the ice. Their sensitive whiskers find shellfish on the seabed.
morses.anecdote: A walrus can eat more than 3,000 shellfish in a single meal.
morses.vedette: They have the coldest pool in the Marine City and love ice-cold showers.

hippocampes.texte: These horse-headed fish swim upright and cling to seaweed with their tail.
hippocampes.anecdote: In seahorses, it's the male who carries the eggs and gives birth.
hippocampes.vedette: They live in small seagrass tanks, at children's eye level.

pieuvres.texte: With three hearts and blue blood, they change colour in an instant. They're also escape champions.
pieuvres.anecdote: Two thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms.
pieuvres.vedette: Their tank is full of hiding places and toys: keepers give them jars to open.

footer.description: In the heart of the Chartreuse mountains, our meerkats and all their friends welcome you in enclosures designed for their well-being. A zoo to enjoy as a family, with free activities every day.

wwf.texte: For more than 60 years, WWF has been working to protect endangered species and their natural habitats, from the African savanna to the oceans. Discover its work and how you too can support it.

engagements.texte: Le Domaine des Suricates takes part in the {lien}. Every birth at the park strengthens a reserve population for threatened species.
Part of every ticket funds projects in the animals' natural habitats: anti-poaching work, reforestation, rescue centres.
Feeding times, animal talks, signs: throughout your visit, our keepers explain what threatens wildlife and how to protect it.
